Long Beach lawmaker has social media bill signed into law

By City News ServiceSeptember 10, 2026Updated:September 10, 2026No Comments2 Mins Read
Facebook Twitter Pinterest LinkedIn Tumblr Email
Share
Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Email

LONG BEACH – Assemblyman Josh Lowenthal, D-Long Beach, hailed the signing Thursday of legislation he authored barring social media platforms from offering certain addictive features to users under 16, part of a package of new California laws aimed at protecting children online.

Gov. Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 1709 in Marin County along with more than a dozen other digital-safety measures. The Lowenthal bill prohibits platforms from offering features defined as psychologically exploitative and designed to maximize engagement in ways that foreseeably lead to compulsive use among children under 16.

Prohibited features include infinite scrolling and algorithmic autoplay, with the state attorney general authorized to define additional features through regulations.

“Today, all of us are saying the same thing,” Lowenthal said. “We’re saying (that) we don’t have to take it anymore, and families in the state of California — you don’t have to take it anymore.”

AB 1709 passed both houses of the Legislature without a dissenting vote.

The measure is the first law of its kind in the nation prohibiting social media platforms from providing addictive features to users under 16. The legislation comes amid growing efforts in the United States and abroad to regulate social media use by children.

The Electronic Frontier Foundation opposed AB 1709, contending the measure could restrict young people’s access to online forums and prompt platforms to use age-verification systems involving government identification or biometric information. The group called the measure a “massive privacy and free speech nightmare.”

Newsom defended the approach, saying the law targets features designed to keep young users engaged rather than imposing a broad social media ban.

“This is about the features themselves,” Newsom said. “This is about addressing the problem: the scrolling, the algorithms. This is about addressing the substantive issue around the engineering.”

Other measures in the package impose restrictions on artificial intelligence chatbots used by children, strengthen youth digital privacy protections and expand laws involving digitally altered or AI-generated child sexual exploitation material.

Lowenthal called the measures a “bold first step.”

“We’re laying the groundwork for what comes next,” Lowenthal said. “Stronger protections. Smarter enforcement. More accountability for the platforms that have treated our children’s attention as a product to be mined.”

OC woman arrested on defrauding high school football team

By City News ServiceSeptember 10, 2026Updated:September 10, 2026No Comments2 Mins Read
Facebook Twitter Pinterest LinkedIn Tumblr Email
Share
Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Email

ALISO VIEJO – A 56-year-old woman was arrested Thursday after being charged in a federal indictment with defrauding a non-profit set up to assist a high school football team, authorities said.

Julie Hanway Molina was arrested at her home and was expected to make an initial court appearance in U.S. District Court in Santa Ana on Thursday to face four counts of wire fraud.

According to federal prosecutors, Molina allegedly served as the organization’s treasurer and used more than $400,000 of its funds to pay off her delinquent home mortgage.

A federal grand jury returned an indictment on September 2 charging Molina with executing a scheme to defraud the nonprofit organization between 2023 and November of 2025 by diverting funds from the group’s bank account for use on her own personal expenses, including the mortgage and credit card bills.

Molina was treasurer of an Aliso Niguel High School football team support organization.

She allegedly wired approximately $131,523 from the bank account in Laguna Hills through Federal Reserve facilities in New Jersey and Texas to an account in Santa Ana and sent emails to the nonprofit’s board members attaching falsified reports.

A total of $411,761 was allegedly misappropriated.

If convicted, Molina could face 20 years in federal prison for each count, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office.
